title: Louvre Reopens Apollo Gallery Without Jewels Nine Months After Heist
excerpt: The Galerie d'Apollon is once again open to visitors, but the surviving crown jewels have been moved to a windowless room after thieves stole $102 million in royal jewellery last October.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • The Louvre's Galerie d'Apollon reopened on July 22, nine months after a $102 million heist.
  • Surviving royal jewels have been relocated to a secure, windowless room in the museum.
  • Four suspects are in custody, but most stolen items remain missing.
  • Former director Laurence des Cars resigned amid criticism over security failures.
The Heist in Numbers
$102 million
Value of Stolen Jewels
8

The Louvre Museum's Apollo Gallery reopened to visitors on Wednesday without any jewels on display, nine months after a daylight robbery of French crown jewels worth $102 million exposed sweeping security failures at the world's most-visited museum.

https://x.com/Reuters/status/2079918132571852906

Visitors can once again walk through the gallery's richly decorated 17th-century interior — one of the Louvre's most celebrated spaces — but the surviving royal jewels have been relocated to a windowless room elsewhere in the Paris museum, according to new Louvre director Christophe Leribault.

A Gallery Reborn — Without Its Treasures

The Galerie d'Apollon, created under King Louis XIV and designed by architect Louis Le Vau, served as the blueprint for the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles. Its ceiling, painted by Charles Le Brun and later completed by Eugène Delacroix, depicts the triumph of the sun — a tribute to the Sun King himself.

“We want visitors to experience it as the most lavish room in the Louvre and rediscover a bit of the palace beneath the museum.”

— Christophe Leribault, Louvre Director

Leribault, appointed in February to lead the museum out of crisis, said the aim was to restore the gallery to its original function as a ceremonial state room rather than simply reopen it with two empty display cases. “The idea is to start afresh,” he told Le Parisien.

The October Heist

In October 2025, two men parked a commercial furniture lift outside the Louvre in broad daylight, rode it up to the second story, smashed a window, and cracked open display cases with angle grinders. They fled on the back of scooters driven by two accomplices. The entire operation lasted less than seven minutes.

The thieves made off with eight pieces of royal jewellery, including tiaras and necklaces worn by French queens. Four people suspected of direct involvement have been charged and placed in custody, but the men claim to have been working for an unidentified mastermind. Police have so far failed to trace either the stolen haul or the purported organiser.

The only recovered item is the Crown of Empress Eugénie, wife of Napoleon III, which was found damaged near the museum after it was apparently dropped during the escape. It is currently undergoing restoration.

A Reckoning for the Louvre

The robbery triggered a political and institutional crisis. Culture Minister Catherine Pegard hailed the gallery's reopening as “the symbol of a new beginning” for the museum after what she called a “trauma for the whole world,” and pledged to strengthen security at museums nationwide.

A damning report by the Cour des Comptes, France's public auditor, found that in the years before the heist the museum had “favoured operations that were visible and attractive” over essential maintenance and security upgrades. Former director Laurence des Cars resigned in February 2026 after facing months of criticism; she had initially offered to resign on the day of the burglary, but President Emmanuel Macron declined the offer at the time.

What Comes Next

Louvre's Security Overhaul
›New surveillance cameras installed.
›Anti-intrusion systems upgraded.
›Part of €800 million renovation plan.
›Dedicated gallery for the Mona Lisa by 2031.

The Louvre has installed additional surveillance cameras and new anti-intrusion systems as part of a broader overhaul. The upgrades fall under the museum's “Louvre New Renaissance” renovation programme, estimated to cost up to 800 million euros ($933 million), which also aims to reduce overcrowding and create a dedicated gallery for the Mona Lisa by 2031.

Leribault pointed to the 2019 theft from Dresden's Green Vault museum as cause for optimism — those stolen 18th-century jewels were largely recovered three years later after the culprits negotiated lighter sentences. Whether the Louvre's missing treasures follow a similar path remains to be seen.
